verdicts.evidence: The label says every documented pairing is 'built on tagged facts in both pieces'. Seven of the nine contain a line the two home pages do not support. (1) FN19 x Same Building: 'The same data center appears twice' - FN19 is Hyperion in Richland Parish, Louisiana; Same Building, Two Bills is about PJM (BGE, Dominion, Washington DC) and never mentions Hyperion, Meta or Louisiana. (2) Check-In x Permanent Record: 'The check-in tag is the first line of the lifelong file' - the home register opens with the baptism record at age 0 ('The first entry in a register'); the check-in log arrives at age 3. (3) Permanent Record x Estate Sale: 'A parish file ... moves to the next parish and stays' - the home page limits this to Baltimore ('When Baltimore's Catholic parishes merged...'); 'most state privacy laws exempt nonprofits' appears on neither page (the home page says only that coverage 'depends on whether that law covers nonprofits at all'). (4) Estate Sale x EP 09: 'that memory is an asset on the company's books' - EP 09 says only 'Character.AI's c.ai+ is $9.99 a month' under a heading about being remembered, and FN20 says customer data 'goes on the list of things it owns' in bankruptcy; neither says the tier buys memory or that memory is booked as an asset. 'HIPAA covers providers, not apps' is on neither page. (5) House x Permanent Record: 'Both institutions score a person's value' and 'a church consultant' - the home page says 'A consultant to nonprofits described what these systems want' and 'This exhibit does not allege that any church or school builds such a profile'; the sportsbook's 'elasticity' model is the New York Times's account of DraftKings, disputed by the company, 'mostly its online casino'. (6) House x Scam: 'Each company runs ... a second, optional one' - the home page finds no harm alarm on record at FanDuel and reports DraftKings's protection model was shelved; in Britain the bank's duty has not been optional since 7 Oct 2024. 'A bank and its customer both want the scam stopped' is not in the home page, whose thesis is that the alarm gets built where the law makes the bank pay. (7) 269-Day Clock x Estate Sale: the question asks why 'destruction is the default' for one and 'sale the default' for the other - the brief documents one destruction order (Crozer, with imaging records sold to ChristianaCare, and Atlanta Medical Center's records kept by Wellstar); FN20 shows one list destroyed and two sold with conditions. No default is documented on either side. Scam x Estate Sale and Vogtle x FN19 hold ('roughly 90 percent borrowed', SB 31 of 2009, Regulation E, 363(b)(1)).
